blocks.text: NAHUM THE ELKOSHITE (NAHUM 1:1) · TWO KINGDOMS
Nahum. “The burden of Nineveh”: the LORD's judgment on the bloody city, and good tidings for Judah.
SCRIPTURE CALLS
Prophet
ERA
Two kingdoms 930–586 BC
IN THE DAYS OF
No ruler named beside him
BOOK
Nahum
HOW THE WORD CAME
The book calls itself both “The burden of Nineveh” and “The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite”.
THE CALL
How the word came
The book calls itself both “The burden of Nineveh” and “The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite”. Nahum 1:1
THE MESSAGE
The word in its main themes
The LORD who is slow to anger, and avenges
“The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked”
Nahum 1:3 (KJV) →
“The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.”
Nahum 1:7 (KJV) →
Good tidings to Judah
“Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!”
Nahum 1:15 (KJV) →
The fall of Nineveh
“Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery”
Nahum 3:1 (KJV) →
“Nineveh is laid waste: who will bemoan her?”
Nahum 3:7 (KJV) →
Like No
THE WORD TO …
To whom the word was spoken
TO NINEVEH
“Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts”
Nahum 2:13 (KJV) →
TO JUDAH
“O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee”
Nahum 1:15 (KJV) →
TO THE KING OF ASSYRIA
“Thy shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria: thy nobles shall dwell in the dust”
Nahum 3:18 (KJV) →
THE BOOK
The book of Nahum
1 Heading Nahum 1:1
2 The LORD who avenges; comfort for Judah Nahum 1:2–15
3 The siege and fall of the city Nahum 2:1–13
4 Woe to the bloody city Nahum 3:1–19
HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
From the textScripture says nothing of Nahum outside the first verse of his book. Nahum 1:1
TRADITION SAYS

A grave at Alkush (Alqosh), near Mosul, “is shown as that of Nahum”.[3] Who says so: A local tradition near Mosul, reported by S. R. Driver (1891), Driver: it “cannot be traced back beyond the 16th cent.”
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
Between the fall of Thebes and the fall of Nineveh
S. R. Driver (1891); A. B. Davidson (1896); G. A. Smith (1898)

Nahum 3:8–10 speaks of No as already carried away. Driver takes No to be Thebes, captured by Ashurbanipal “shortly after 664”, and the latest limit to be Nineveh's fall, which he and Davidson dated about 607–606. Driver: “Within these limits it is impossible to fix the date more precisely.” Nahum 3:8–10 [3][46][45]
Soon after Sennacherib's defeat, under Hezekiah
C. F. Keil (1868), following Vitringa
Keil quotes Vitringa: “the date of Nahum must be fixed a very short time after Isaiah and Micah, and therefore in the reign of Hezekiah”.[10]
In Manasseh's reign
Seder Olam, a Jewish chronology ascribed by Jewish authorities to Rabbi Jose ben Halafta, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1905)
It places “those of Joel, Nahum, and Habakkuk in the reign of Manasseh.”[42]
IN SCRIPTURE
Every passage
CHAPTERS · 3
Nahum 1 Nahum 2 Nahum 3
PASSAGES · 1
WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture gives no call, no king and no date for Nahum, and nothing of his life.
Scripture does not record the fall of Nineveh.
The New Testament does not quote Nahum. Romans 10:15's “How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace” is closest in wording to Isaiah 52:7; Nahum 1:15 has a similar line.
